books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: This map, titled “Territory of Louisiana 1803–1819,” shows the Louisiana Purchase territory shaded red and labeled “LOUISIANA PURCHASE.” A note in the corner reads: “Louisiana Purchase Territory ceded by FRANCE to the UNITED STATES by treaty of April 30, 1803, as asserted and maintained by the American Government.” The shaded land stretches from the Mississippi River west to the Rocky Mountains and from the Gulf of Mexico north to Canada. New Orleans sits at the mouth of the Mississippi River.
stimulus.source_note: Map of the Louisiana Purchase Territory, National Archives (NARA 594889); public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The map best supports which of the following conclusions about the Louisiana Purchase?

options.text: It gave the United States its first port on the Pacific Ocean
options.misconception: The shaded land reaches the Rocky Mountains, not the Pacific; the Oregon Country came later.

options.text: It roughly doubled the size of the United States
It was purchased from Spain after the War of 1812
options.misconception: The corner note says the land was ceded by France in 1803, nine years before the war.

options.text: It settled the boundary between the United States and Canada
options.misconception: The northern boundary stayed unsettled; Oregon and the 49th parallel came decades later.

rationales.A: The purchase reached the Rocky Mountains, not the Pacific coast. A Pacific port came only with the Oregon settlement of 1846.
rationales.B: The red shading covers land as large as the United States itself, from the Mississippi to the Rockies. One purchase nearly doubled the country.
rationales.C: The corner note names France, not Spain, and dates the treaty April 30, 1803, nine years before the War of 1812 began.
rationales.D: The map shows the purchase, not a settled northern border. The Canadian boundary in the West was fixed only with the Oregon compromise of 1846.
rationales.general:
1. Read the corner note. The land was “ceded by FRANCE to the UNITED STATES by treaty of April 30, 1803.”
2. Look at the size. The red shading runs from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains, a stretch as large as the United States itself.
3. Put it together. Buying land that big in one stroke nearly doubled the nation's size.
Background: The purchase cost $15 million, and Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark to explore the new land.
Remember: when a map shades a huge new territory, ask how much it changed the country's size.

figures.caption: Territory of Louisiana, 1803–1819, showing the Louisiana Purchase
figures.alt: Map of the United States with the Louisiana Purchase territory shaded red from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains
